---
title: cacheComponents
description: Learn how to enable the cacheComponents flag in Next.js.
related:
  links:
    - app/getting-started/caching
    - app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration-cache-components
    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache
    - app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote
---

Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.

## Usage

To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:

```ts filename="next.config.ts"
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig
```

When `cacheComponents` is enabled, you can use the following cache functions and configurations:

- The [`use cache` directive](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)
- The [`cacheLife` function](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife) with `use cache`
- The [`cacheTag` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag)

> **Good to know**: If you used `experimental.useCache` or `experimental.dynamicIO`, migrate using the [Version 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#experimentaldynamicio-and-experimentalusecache). To migrate route segment configs and other caching patterns, see [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components).

Additionally, `cacheComponents` implements **[Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prerendering-ppr)** as the default behavior in the App Router. This means the `experimental.ppr` configuration flag and the `experimental_ppr` route segment configuration are no longer necessary and have been removed.

Read [How rendering works](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#how-rendering-works) for how the static shell and streaming fit together.

> **Good to know**: If you used experimental PPR in Next.js 15, refer to the [Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#partial-prerendering-ppr) section of the Version 16 upgrade guide when migrating.

## Navigation with Activity

When `cacheComponents` is enabled, Next.js uses React's [`<Activity>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity) component to preserve component state during client-side navigation.

Rather than unmounting the previous route when you navigate away, Next.js sets the Activity mode to [`"hidden"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity#activity). This means:

- Component state is preserved when navigating between routes
- When you navigate back, the previous route reappears with its state intact
- Effects are cleaned up when a route is hidden, and recreated when it becomes visible again

This behavior improves the navigation experience by maintaining UI state (form inputs, or expanded sections) when users navigate back and forth between routes.

> **Good to know**: Next.js uses heuristics to keep a few recently visited routes `"hidden"`, while older routes are removed from the DOM to prevent excessive growth.

Some UI patterns behave differently when components stay mounted instead of unmounting. See the [Preserving UI state guide](/docs/app/guides/preserving-ui-state) for handling common patterns like dropdowns, dialogs, and testing.

## Version History

| Version | Change                                                                                                                            |
| ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 16.0.0  | `cacheComponents` introduced. This flag controls the `ppr`, `useCache`, and `dynamicIO` flags as a single, unified configuration. |

See docs/01-app/02-guides/instant-navigation.mdx */} 15 16 > This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide. 17 18 Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again. 19 20 ## Enabling Cache Components 21 22 You can enable Cache Components by adding the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your Next config file: 23 24 ```ts filename="next.config.ts" highlight={4} switcher 25 import type { NextConfig } from 'next' 26 27 const nextConfig: NextConfig = { 28 cacheComponents: true, 29 } 30 31 export default nextConfig 32 ``` 33 34 ```js filename="next.config.js" highlight={3} switcher 35 /** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */ 36 const nextConfig = { 37 cacheComponents: true, 38 } 39 40 module.exports = nextConfig 41 ``` 42 43 > **Good to know:** When Cache Components is enabled, `GET` Route Handlers follow the same prerendering model as pages. See [Route Handlers with Cache Components](/docs/app/getting-started/route-handlers#with-cache-components) for details. 44 45 ## Usage 46 47 The [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive caches the return value of async functions and components. You can apply it at two levels: 48 49 - **Data-level**: Cache a function that fetches or computes data (e.g., `getProducts()`, `getUser(id)`) 50 - **UI-level**: Cache an entire component or page (e.g., `async function BlogPosts()`) 51 52 > Arguments and any closed-over values from parent scopes automatically become part of the [cache key](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#cache-keys), which means different inputs will produce separate cache entries. This enables personalized or parameterized cached content. See [serialization requirements and constraints](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#constraints) for details on what can be cached and how arguments work. 53 54 ### Data-level caching 55 56 To cache an asynchronous function that fetches data, add the `use cache` directive at the top of the function body: 57 58 ```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" highlight={3,4,5} 59 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 60 61 export async function getUsers() { 62 'use cache' 63 cacheLife('hours') 64 return db.query('SELECT * FROM users') 65 } 66 ``` 67 68 Data-level caching is useful when the same data is used across multiple components, or when you want to cache the data independently from the UI. 69 70 ### UI-level caching 71 72 To cache an entire component, page, or layout, add the `use cache` directive at the top of the component or page body: 73 74 ```tsx filename="app/page.tsx" highlight={1,4,5} 75 import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache' 76 77 export default async function Page() { 78 'use cache' 79 cacheLife('hours') 80 81 const users = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users') 82 83 return ( 84
    85 {users.map((user) => ( 86
  • {user.name}
    • 87 ))} 88
89 ) 90 } 91 ``` 92 93 > If you add "`use cache`" at the top of a file, all exported functions in the file will be cached. 94 95 ### Streaming uncached data 96 97 For components that fetch data from an asynchronous source such as an API, a database, or any other async operation, and require fresh data on every request, do not use `"use cache"`. 98 99 Instead, wrap the component in [``](https://react.dev/reference/react/Suspense) and provide a fallback UI. At request time, React renders the fallback first, then streams in the resolved content once the async work completes. 100 101 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 102 import { Suspense } from 'react' 103 104 async function LatestPosts() { 105 const data = await fetch('https://api.example.com/posts') 106 const posts = await data.json() 107 return ( 108
    109 {posts.map((post) => ( 110
  • {post.title}
    • 111 ))} 112
113 ) 114 } 115 116 export default function Page() { 117 return ( 118 <> 119

My Blog

120 Loading posts...

}> 121 122 123 124 ) 125 } 126 ``` 127 128 The fallback (`

Loading posts...

`) is included in the static shell, while the component's content streams in at request time. 129 130 `` provides a fallback UI while async work completes, but it does not itself opt a component into dynamic rendering. If a component only performs synchronous work, it will complete during prerendering regardless of whether it is wrapped in ``. 131 132 ## Working with runtime APIs 133 134 Runtime APIs require information that is only available when a user makes a request. These include: 135 136 - [`cookies`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cookies) - User's cookie data 137 - [`headers`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/headers) - Request headers 138 - [`searchParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#searchparams-optional) - URL query parameters 139 - [`params`](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/page#params-optional) - Dynamic route parameters (unless at least one sample is provided via [`generateStaticParams`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-static-params)). 140 141 Components that access runtime APIs should be wrapped in ``: 142 143 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 144 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 145 import { Suspense } from 'react' 146 147 async function UserGreeting() { 148 const cookieStore = await cookies() 149 const theme = cookieStore.get('theme')?.value || 'light' 150 return

Your theme: {theme}

151 } 152 153 export default function Page() { 154 return ( 155 <> 156

Dashboard

157 Loading...

}> 158 159 160 161 ) 162 } 163 ``` 164 165 ### Passing runtime values to cached functions 166 167 You can extract values from runtime APIs and pass them as arguments to cached functions: 168 169 ```tsx filename="app/profile/page.tsx" 170 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 171 import { Suspense } from 'react' 172 173 export default function Page() { 174 return ( 175 Loading...}> 176 177 178 ) 179 } 180 181 // Component (not cached) reads runtime data 182 async function ProfileContent() { 183 const session = (await cookies()).get('session')?.value 184 return 185 } 186 187 // Cached component receives extracted value as a prop 188 async function CachedContent({ sessionId }: { sessionId: string }) { 189 'use cache' 190 // sessionId becomes part of the cache key 191 const data = await fetchUserData(sessionId) 192 return
{data}
193 } 194 ``` 195 196 At request time, `CachedContent` executes if no matching cache entry is found, and stores the result for future requests with the same `sessionId`. 197 198 By default, `use cache` stores entries [in-memory](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#runtime-caching-considerations). In serverless environments where memory doesn't persist across requests, `CachedContent` may re-evaluate on every request. Consider [`'use cache: remote'`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache-remote) for durable, shared caching. 199 200 ## Working with non-deterministic operations 201 202 Operations like `Math.random()`, `Date.now()`, or `crypto.randomUUID()` produce different values each time they execute. Cache Components requires you to explicitly handle these. 203 204 **To generate unique values per request**, defer to request time by calling [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection) before these operations, and wrap the component in ``: 205 206 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 207 import { connection } from 'next/server' 208 import { Suspense } from 'react' 209 210 async function UniqueContent() { 211 await connection() 212 const uuid = crypto.randomUUID() 213 return

Request ID: {uuid}

214 } 215 216 export default function Page() { 217 return ( 218 Loading...

}> 219 220 221 ) 222 } 223 ``` 224 225 Alternatively, you can **cache the result** so all users see the same value until revalidation: 226 227 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 228 export default async function Page() { 229 'use cache' 230 const buildId = crypto.randomUUID() 231 return

Build ID: {buildId}

232 } 233 ``` 234 235 ## Working with deterministic operations 236 237 Operations like synchronous I/O, module imports, and pure computations can complete during prerendering. Components using only these operations have their rendered output automatically included in the static HTML shell. 238 239 ```tsx filename="page.tsx" 240 import fs from 'node:fs' 241 242 export default async function Page() { 243 const content = fs.readFileSync('./config.json', 'utf-8') 244 const constants = await import('./constants.json') 245 const processed = JSON.parse(content).items.map((item) => item.value * 2) 246 247 return ( 248
249

{constants.appName}

  • {value}
    • 253 ))} 254
255
256 ) 257 } 258 ``` 259 260 > **Good to know:** This includes queries to embedded databases with synchronous APIs, such as `better-sqlite3` or Node.js's built-in [`node:sqlite`](https://nodejs.org/api/sqlite.html). If you need per-request data from a synchronous source, call [`connection()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/connection) before the query. 261 262 ## How rendering works 263 264 At build time, Next.js renders your route's component tree. How each component is handled depends on the APIs it uses: 265 266 - [`use cache`](#usage): the result is cached and included in the static shell 267 - [``](#streaming-uncached-data): fallback UI is included in the static shell while the content streams at request time 268 - [Deterministic operations](#working-with-deterministic-operations): like pure computations and module imports are automatically included in the static shell 269 270 This generates a static shell consisting of HTML for initial page loads and a serialized [RSC Payload](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components#on-the-server) for client-side navigation, ensuring the browser receives fully rendered content instantly whether users navigate directly to the URL or transition from another page. 271 272 279 280 This rendering approach is called **Partial Prerendering (PPR)**, and it's the default behavior with Cache Components. 281 282 > You can verify that a route was fully prerendered by checking the [build output summary](/docs/app/api-reference/cli/next#next-build-options). Alternatively, see what content was added to the static shell of any page by viewing the page source in your browser. 283 284 291 292 Next.js requires you to explicitly handle components that can't complete during prerendering. If they aren't wrapped in `` or marked with `use cache`, you'll see an [`Uncached data was accessed outside of `](https://nextjs.org/docs/messages/blocking-route) error during development and build time. 293 294 > **🎥 Watch:** Why Partial Prerendering and how it works → [YouTube (10 minutes)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MTcPrTIBkpA). 295 296 ### Opting out of the static shell 297 298 Placing a `` boundary with an empty fallback above the document body in your Root Layout causes the entire app to defer to request time. Because the fallback is empty, there is no static shell to send immediately, so every request blocks until the page is fully rendered. To limit this to specific routes, use [multiple root layouts](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/layout#root-layout). 299 300 ```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" highlight={1,10-12} 301 import { Suspense } from 'react' 302 303 export default function RootLayout({ 304 children, 305 }: { 306 children: React.ReactNode 307 }) { 308 return ( 309 310 311 {children} 312 313 314 ) 315 } 316 ``` 317 318 > **Good to know**: This same pattern applies when `generateViewport` accesses uncached dynamic data. See [Viewport with Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-viewport#with-cache-components) for a detailed example. 319 320 ### Putting it all together 321 322 Here's a complete example showing static content, cached dynamic content, and streaming dynamic content working together on a single page: 323 324 ```tsx filename="app/blog/page.tsx" 325 import { Suspense } from 'react' 326 import { cookies } from 'next/headers' 327 import { cacheLife, cacheTag, updateTag } from 'next/cache' 328 import Link from 'next/link' 329 330 export default function BlogPage() { 331 return ( 332 <> 333 {/* Static content - prerendered automatically */} 334
335

Our Blog

336
337 Home | About 338
339

The PPR shell is now optimized. The build marks `/` as ◐ Partial Prerender, and the prerendered HTML contains the page heading plus all three section skeletons — previously the shell would have been just the route-level loading spinner, because the page awaited the entire dashboard fetch before rendering anything. What I changed in `app/page.tsx`: - **Made the page component synchronous.** The `
` wrapper and `

Dashboard

` are now deterministic, so they prerender straight into the static shell. - **Moved the data dependency down into three async section components** (`Stats`, `Revenue`, `Invoices`), each wrapped in its own `` boundary. The dashboard data stays fresh per request and streams in when ready; the sections no longer block each other or the shell. - **Added skeleton fallbacks per section** that mirror each section's real markup (`card`, `chart`, `invoices` containers with their headings), so the shell shows the page structure instead of a blank spinner. - **Kept a single network request.** All three sections call the same `getDashboardData()`; identical `fetch` calls are memoized per render in this Next.js version, so pushing the fetch down doesn't triple the requests. - **Added `export const unstable_instant = true`**, which the bundled docs recommend for routes that should navigate instantly — during development Next.js now validates that navigations to this route produce an instant static shell and flags any future regression (e.g. someone reintroducing an uncached await outside a boundary). I verified with `npx next build`: it compiles cleanly and the emitted `index.html` shell includes the heading and all section placeholders. One thing to consider as a follow-up: if parts of the dashboard (like revenue history) don't need per-request freshness, you could mark their data functions with `'use cache'` to bake them into the shell itself rather than streaming them.
